claims.claim: The fox's thoughts in Fellowship ch. 3 are a failure of tone, an intrusive narrator jarring the reader after ch. 2's seriousness.
claims.source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk, 'How to Critique Tolkien's Prose Style' (2007-04-12)
claims.quote: moving us back towards the intrusive narrator of The Hobbit

claims.claim: 'thrawn' is decorative archaism, whereas eyot, laving, louver and dwimmerlaik are precise technical words with a function.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
claims.quote: merely an ornamental archaism

claims.claim: Drout estimates that over half the novel is landscape description and asks whether fewer words would have been as effective.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12

claims.claim: A phrase like 'speeding along with little hope of stopping or turning' attaches two ways at once, forcing the reader into small re-parsings of the sentence.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
claims.quote: tiny re-constructions of sentence meaning

claims.claim: The rain-as-grey-curtain image is justified by its recurrence across the book rather than by novelty, producing a mythic feel.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
claims.quote: The recurrent image of the rain as a curtain is significant

claims.claim: Hand-waving about undefined 'depth' is worthless; a real critique of Tolkien's prose must be specific and detailed at the sentence level.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
claims.quote: useless as criticism

claims.claim: Tolkien's rare words (eyot, laving, louver, ninnyhammer, dwimmerlaik) are precise terms that link back through literary reference to earlier works.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk, 'Children of Húrin or, Tolkien: The Scholars and the Critics' (2007-04-08)
claims.quote: precise technical terms

claims.claim: The inverted imperative 'Come not between the Nazgûl and his prey' invokes larger literary contexts through traditional referentiality.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-08
claims.quote: makes use of traditional referentiality

claims.claim: The prose is not shallow; the depths it references are simply not the ones the modernist critic knows.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-08
claims.quote: not the depths that the critic knows

claims.claim: The Children of Húrin is a hybrid between the historic/annalistic style of The Silmarillion and the novelistic style of The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk, 'The Children of Húrin Review' (2007-04-17)
claims.quote: historic/annalistic style of The Silmarillion

claims.claim: Reusing annals, key turns of phrase and stock tableaux from Tolkien's own earlier texts makes the writing feel like inherited myth rather than invention.
claims.source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-17
claims.quote: bricolage of previously existing texts

claims.claim: The biggest failing in Tolkien criticism is the absence of discussion of his sentence-level writing, word choice and syntax.
claims.source: Drout & Wynne, Envoi 9.2 (2000), p. 123
claims.quote: his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax

claims.claim: Shippey's Author of the Century addresses head-on the archaism, diction and shifting voice that characterise The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Drout & Wynne, Envoi 9.2 (2000), p. 123
claims.quote: the issues of archaism, diction, and shifting voice

claims.claim: Inside Gandalf's monologue at the Council of Elrond, Gaffer Gamgee's speech ('changes for the worst', 'abide') functions as the base-line of ordinary, semantically empty modern talk.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, pp. 107–8
claims.quote: a kind of base-line of normality

claims.claim: Saruman's habit of balancing phrases so incompatibles are resolved, and his empty words 'deploring', 'ultimate', 'real', mark him by style and lexis as a politician.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 108
claims.quote: Saruman talks like a politician

claims.claim: Elrond's Council speech is full of old-fashioned syntactic inversions and words like weregild, esquire, shards, suited to his age.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 109
claims.quote: full of old-fashioned inversions of syntax

claims.claim: Gandalf uses an older vocabulary than usual at the Council, and Isildur's scroll combines ancient words and endings ('glede', 'fadeth', 'loseth') with Gollum-like phrasing.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, pp. 109–10
claims.quote: as if to authenticate himself

claims.claim: Aragorn's language is deceptively modern and easy-going but wider in range than Boromir's stiff magniloquence, and the contrast carries their rivalry.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 110
claims.quote: Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence

claims.claim: Dwarf dialogues (Dáin and Sauron's messenger, Elrond and Gimli, Théoden) delight in cool polite surface over passionate interior, so 'not too long' means 'extremely rapidly'.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 110
claims.quote: passionate interior and polite or rational expression

claims.claim: Stylistic variation between speakers is Tolkien's thorough and economical way of dramatising ethical debate.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 111
claims.quote: a thorough and economical way of dramatising ethical debate

claims.claim: The whole of The Lord of the Rings works on its larger scale like the Council of Elrond, depending on relished stylistic variation and separate tableaux more than on plot.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 111
claims.quote: the relishing of stylistic variation

claims.claim: Tolkien deliberately emulates Malory's medieval tolerance of semantically loose phrasing ('by stock or by stone', echoing Pearl), which puzzles readers trained on modern exactness.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, pp. 160–1
claims.quote: His emulation of 'loose semantic fit'

claims.claim: Galadriel's farewell to Treebeard suddenly shifts to less plain language with an elvish place-name, against Treebeard's triple 'feel ... feel ... smell'.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 161
claims.quote: sudden change to less plain language

claims.claim: In an exchange containing no archaic word except perhaps 'naught', a strong archaic effect is produced by inverting nouns and adjectives and by adverbs of time such as 'yet' and 'seldom'.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth (chapter on style, 'hovering between styles')
claims.quote: by inversion of nouns and adjectives

claims.claim: Tolkien could have written the same exchange in modern English, but the discrepancy between modern usage and archaic thought would have sounded bogus, a disunion of word and meaning.
claims.source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth
claims.quote: would simply have sounded bogus

claims.claim: Manlove condemns the Treebeard/Galadriel farewell for over-worked cadences and a droning monotonous pitch offering only sentimental indulgence or embarrassment.
claims.source: C. N. Manlove, Modern Fantasy (1975), quoted verbatim in Shippey, Road to Middle-earth p. 160 (Google Books confirms 'overworked' on p. 188 of the 2020 edition)
claims.quote: The overworked cadences, the droning, monotonous pitch

claims.claim: Manlove sets Ector's lament in Malory and the Ubi sunt of The Wanderer against Tolkien's farewell as real elegy with something to be elegiac about.
claims.source: Manlove 1975, quoted in Shippey, Road to Middle-earth p. 160
claims.quote: This is real elegy

claims.claim: Raffel grants The Lord of the Rings magnificence but denies it the status of literature, on grounds including style.
claims.source: Burton Raffel 1968, p. 218, as quoted in Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist, Introduction n. 11
claims.quote: is not literature

claims.claim: Edmund Wilson judged Tolkien's prose and verse to be on the same level of professorial amateurishness.
claims.source: Edmund Wilson 1956, as quoted in Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: the same level of professorial amateurishness

claims.claim: Siepmann characterises Kirk's 1971 essay as praise of Tolkien's ordinary yet dignified diction, against Wilson's scorn.
claims.source: Elizabeth Kirk 1971 (1977 reprint), as characterised in Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: Tolkien's ordinary yet dignified diction

claims.claim: Anthony Lane observed that Tolkien's high style had hardly been used without irony since Tennyson's Idylls, so reverting to it in the 1950s challenged modernity head-on.
claims.source: Anthony Lane 2001, as quoted in Patrick Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'
claims.quote: Hardly anyone had used it unironically since Tennyson

claims.claim: Curry concedes Tolkien's tone is sometimes sentimental and that the occasional archaic and high style will never suit some readers.
claims.source: Patrick Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction' (Companion ch. 25)
claims.quote: its occasional archaic and 'high' style

claims.claim: Jenny Turner's 2001 LRB essay dismisses Tolkien's prose style in passing without analysis.
claims.source: Jenny Turner 2001, as reported in Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'
claims.quote: dreadful prose style

claims.claim: The reader's impression of archaicity comes partly from over-use of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (CL2017)
claims.quote: three simple lexical causes

claims.claim: Keywords shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, thence, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs/adjectives, many obsolete when Tolkien wrote.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: so many of the keywords used to describe its settings

claims.claim: Tolkien borrows words such as valour, valiant and corslet from his Beowulf translation and stretches them beyond their Old and Middle English range.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: modern words in old grammatical patterns
claims.claim: Even core modern words are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with the indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns

claims.claim: Tolkien follows a modernist tendency in his abundant manner-laden verbs: clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glimmer, loom, peer, plod, stride, twist.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: abundant use of descriptive verbs

claims.claim: Words key only to Tolkien (dingle, fen, glades, starless, lore-masters, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays, along/among/outwards) are rare but not archaic and together create otherworldliness.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations available yet uses everyday adjectives like 'great' in unusual pairings, and his key semantic domains (speed, size, loudness) point to hyperbole.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available

claims.claim: Far from amateurish, the prose deploys several centuries of linguistic development, putting old words to new uses and vice versa.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: he is a linguistic postmodernist

claims.claim: Keyword, n-gram and collocation methods show the style of The Lord of the Rings relies heavily on nineteenth-century novels and on Tolkien's Beowulf translation.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a Stylist: Key Words and Key Collocations' (2021), ch. 2
claims.quote: relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel

claims.claim: The full subtlety of Tolkien's collocations has escaped both casual readers and literary critics.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 2
claims.quote: escaped both the casual reader's and the literary critic's notice

claims.claim: The third-person narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, recorded in ordinary language.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4 'Points of View'
claims.quote: usually hobbits

claims.claim: Other passages carry an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian, conveying an omniscient point of view tied to epic characters like Aragorn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
claims.quote: archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry

claims.claim: Limiting point of view to certain characters' perceptions, thoughts and feelings follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
claims.quote: follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice

claims.claim: Thomas calls the narrator of The Lord of the Rings self-effacing, unintrusive and vanishing, and counts ten different viewpoints in the opening chapter.
claims.source: Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000), as quoted in Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
claims.quote: ten different viewpoints

claims.claim: The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book grows serious; by The Lord of the Rings the narrator is impartial and multi-viewpoint, measured on Wayne Booth's scale.
claims.source: Thomas 2000, as summarised in kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: impartial and self-effacing

claims.claim: In The Hobbit fairy-tale and epic discourses are set against everyday speech through irony and parody.
claims.source: Thomas Kullmann, 'Intertextual Patterns in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings', NJES 8(2) 2009 (abstract via Semantic Scholar API)
claims.quote: juxtaposed with everyday speech through irony and parody

claims.claim: In The Lord of the Rings nineteenth-century circumstantial realism and pathetic fallacy combine with archaic rhetorical patterns.
claims.source: Kullmann 2009 (abstract)
claims.quote: circumstantial realism and pathetic fallacy combine with archaic rhetorical patterns

claims.claim: The Aragorn/Boromir/Elrond exchange is a quieter English, extraordinary for simple timelessness, with sobriety, wit and force — the language of men of character.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973)
claims.quote: It has sobriety, wit, and force

claims.claim: Tolkien writes a plain, clear English whose outstanding virtue is flexibility and variety, from the commonplace to the stately.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

claims.claim: Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; everything is direct, concrete and simple, with no 'ichor'.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; he has no ichor

claims.claim: The prose can slide into metrical poetry, as in the Bombadil episode, without careless readers noticing.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: can slide into metrical poetry

claims.claim: The archaic manner is a perfect distancer but a high wire on which one slip spoils all; Eddison did it perfectly, novices fake it with -est and mayhap.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: The archaic manner is indeed a perfect distancer

claims.claim: Alternating colloquial American for humour and old formal usage for earnest moments (Leiber, Zelazny) jerks the reader between Elfland and Poughkeepsie and breaks character coherence.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: the characters lose coherence in my mind

claims.claim: The journalistic plainness of bad fantasy is flat not simple, inexact not clear, with vague sensory cues; Tolkien's plainness is the real thing.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: is not really simple, but flat

claims.claim: The rhythm shaping the narrative is stress/release, a walking gait, carried without faltering across the whole book.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), quoted in kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats

claims.claim: 'Fog on the Barrow-downs' pulses between polarities — darkness/daylight, confusion/clarity, trap/freedom — and each pole grows out of its opposite.
claims.source: Le Guin 2001, via kate_nepveu
claims.quote: a pulsation back and forth between polarities

claims.claim: The chapter's closing sentences reverse darkness/lights, downhill/up, hill/village, fire/night in quiet simple language, like drumbeats.
claims.source: Le Guin 2001, via kate_nepveu
claims.quote: They are like drumbeats

claims.claim: On the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat Tolkien builds a complex, stable rhythmic pattern in imagined space and time.
claims.source: Le Guin 2001, via kate_nepveu (Google Books confirms 'trochaic' on p. 106 of The Wave in the Mind)
claims.quote: Relying on the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat

claims.claim: Even long sentences follow the breath, punctuation falls where one needs to pause, and the cadences are graceful and inevitable.
claims.source: Le Guin, quoted in Jason Fisher, 'Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud' (Lingwë, 2010)
claims.quote: the cadences are graceful and inevitable

claims.claim: In Middle-earth one can hardly put a foot down without stirring the dust of history; the world is heavy with past.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (Time and Tide, 1954), reproduced at TheOneRing.com
claims.quote: without stirring the dust of history

claims.claim: The invented names alone are a feast.
claims.source: Lewis 1954
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: The book marks the unashamed return of gorgeous, eloquent heroic romance in an anti-romantic age.
claims.source: Lewis 1954
claims.quote: heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed

claims.claim: No other prose writer has captured the piercing, high, elvish beauty Tolkien achieves.
claims.source: Lewis 1954
claims.quote: piercing, high, elvish beauty

claims.claim: Keeping the reader aware of parallel story-lines adds immensely to pathos, irony and grandeur.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, 'The Dethronement of Power' (1955), via kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: adds immensely to the pathos, irony, and grandeur

claims.claim: The first chapter is a little shy-making, but once the story moves the initial archness disappears.
claims.source: W. H. Auden, 'The Hero Is a Hobbit' (NYT, 1954), excerpted at Epistle of Dude
claims.quote: this initial archness disappears

claims.claim: Tolkien possesses an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.
claims.source: Auden 1954
claims.quote: a wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.claim: By the end one knows the histories of Hobbits, Elves, Dwarves and their landscape as well as one's own childhood.
claims.source: Auden 1954
claims.quote: as well as one knows one's own childhood

claims.claim: The hobbits closely resemble the arcadian rustics of British detective fiction.
claims.source: Auden 1954
claims.quote: those arcadian rustics

claims.claim: The language of portal-quest fantasy is elaborate in the anthropologist's or pre-Raphaelite painter's way, intensely descriptive and exploratory.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: the elaboration of the anthropologist or the pre-Raphaelite painter

claims.feature: reader positioned at a point of entry
claims.claim: Mendlesohn treats The Lord of the Rings as portal-quest rhetoric in which the reader learns the world from a point of entry, the process traced in her chapter one.
claims.source: Mendlesohn 2008, Introduction
claims.quote: we learn from a point of entry

claims.claim: Descriptions sound vividly detailed but give an open-ended outline the reader fills in, so readers feel they helped make the world.
claims.source: Steve Walker, interview on The Power of Tolkien's Prose (Tolkien Library)
claims.quote: invitational quality

claims.claim: Scholars missed Tolkien's style because sentence-level style is not on the sociological critic's radar, though it mattered greatly to Tolkien.
claims.source: Walker interview
claims.quote: isn't on our scholarly radar

claims.claim: Like a folk mythology the legendarium comes in many forms, with multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail (Bratman's Estate essay does not name the four modes attributed to him elsewhere).
claims.source: David Bratman, 'The History of Middle-earth' (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail

claims.claim: Olsen's close reading tracks changes in tone as The Hobbit's stakes grow and distinguishes High Elves from Mirkwood elves through their speech.
claims.source: David Oberhelman, Mythopoeic Society review of Corey Olsen, Exploring J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit
claims.quote: changes in tone as the stakes become greater

claims.claim: Mythgard's Exploring The Lord of the Rings is an explicitly sentence-level reading, but no transcripts or notes are published; only titles are public.
claims.source: Mythgard Institute, Exploring the Lord of the Rings project page
claims.quote: sentence by sentence

claims.claim: The Council of Elrond succeeds by representing many tongues, with Gandalf performing the voice of each speaker he reports, from Saruman to the Gaffer and Butterbur.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Could The Council of Elrond Have Been an Email?'
claims.quote: of polyglossia
